title: Embedded Execution Models and System Partitioning

standard.family: AutoLeaP Embedded Systems Body of Knowledge

summary: An embedded product is best understood as an end-to-end execution system, not as a collection of processors and software layers. Inputs arrive through sensors, networks or user interaction; software transforms them under timing and resource constraints; outputs affect displays, actuators, storage or cloud services. The architecture must therefore define where each responsibility executes, how it communicates, and what happens when a layer is unavailable.
learningObjectives: Differentiate bare-metal, RTOS, Embedded Linux and Android execution models.
Select boundaries using timing, isolation, lifecycle and product constraints.
Explain how hardware/software partitioning affects ownership, verification and future reuse.
explanation: An embedded product is best understood as an end-to-end execution system, not as a collection of processors and software layers. Inputs arrive through sensors, networks or user interaction; software transforms them under timing and resource constraints; outputs affect displays, actuators, storage or cloud services. The architecture must therefore define where each responsibility executes, how it communicates, and what happens when a layer is unavailable.

Bare-metal firmware offers minimal overhead and direct control but places scheduling, concurrency and lifecycle discipline on the product code. An RTOS adds deterministic task and resource abstractions. Embedded Linux adds process isolation, a rich driver and networking ecosystem, and a long-lived platform lifecycle. Android adds framework services, application lifecycle, permissions and a product-facing ecosystem above Linux. A heterogeneous product may use all four across separate cores or devices.

Partitioning should begin with product behavior, deadlines, fault containment, security boundaries, update cadence and organizational ownership. Hardware acceleration, firmware, platform services and applications are implementation choices made after those constraints are visible. The strongest architecture keeps product intent separate from hardware details while preserving explicit contracts for timing, data freshness, authority and degradation.
whyItMatters: Poor partitioning creates hidden cross-layer dependencies, long integration cycles and release risk.
A stable execution model allows common features to scale across products without forcing every product into the same hardware configuration.
inputs: Product use cases and customer outcomes
Timing, safety, security and availability constraints
activities: Map end-to-end data and control paths
Allocate responsibilities to hardware, firmware, OS services and applications
Define interfaces, lifecycle and degraded behavior
Review reversibility, testability and product-family reuse
outputs: Architecture decision records and open assumptions
automotiveExample: A connected machine platform uses an MCU for a 1 ms actuator loop, Embedded Linux for gateway and telematics services, and Android for operator HMI. The MCU remains the final authority for actuator limits. Linux publishes validated state through a versioned service, while Android requests user-level actions through the platform API. Loss of Linux or Android does not remove local control safety.
commonMistakes: Selecting an operating system before defining deadlines and failure behavior
Putting product policy into board-specific firmware because it is convenient
Assuming a faster SoC removes the need for timing and contention analysis
Treating organizational boundaries as architecture boundaries without technical review
Consolidating mixed-criticality workloads without proving isolation
